# Where this fits

## Seven weeks, one model at a time {.smaller}

| Week | Model | What it assumes |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 3 | the benchmarks | the future looks like one simple rule |
| 2 | decomposition | one season, one trend |
| 4 | ETS | one short season, one level, one slope |
| 5 | regression | the calendar and the predictors explain the series |
| 6, 7 | ARIMA, SARIMA, dynamic regression | one seasonal period, and the error is ARIMA |

## What this lecture is for {.smaller}

What none of those models handles well — one tool for each, with a worked example and an honest
scorecard:

1. **More than one season at once** — hourly data have a day *and* a week *and* a year. *MSTL,
   harmonic regression, Prophet.*
2. **A year that is not a whole number of weeks** — weekly data. *Fourier terms with $P = 52.18$.*
3. **Not knowing which model is right** — and having to pick one anyway. *Combinations, and how to put
   an interval around one.*
4. **Forecasts that must stay within limits** — prices cannot go negative. *Transformations.*
5. **Series that are mostly zeros** — slow-moving stock. *Croston and its relatives.*
6. **A gap at the start, not the end.** *Backcasting.*

The third — **combining forecasts** — is the one that matters most for your own series, and for
Lab 8.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading

[FPP3 §12.1 complex seasonality](https://otexts.com/fpp3/complexseasonality.html) ·
[§13.2 counts](https://otexts.com/fpp3/counts.html) ·
[§13.3 limits](https://otexts.com/fpp3/limits.html) ·
[§13.4 combinations](https://otexts.com/fpp3/combinations.html) ·

# Complex seasonality

## Half-hourly electricity demand {.smaller}

Victoria, Australia — the series from Week 7, now at its native frequency: one value every 30 minutes,
September to mid-December 2014.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
vic = pd.read_csv('../data/vic_elec.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
wide = vic.pivot_table(index="ds", columns="unique_id", values="y").reset_index()
elec = wide[(wide["ds"] >= "2014-09-01") & (wide["ds"] < "2014-12-21")].reset_index(drop=True)
y_el = elec["Demand"].to_numpy(float) / 1000                  # GW
temp = elec["Temperature"].to_numpy(float)
print(f"{len(elec)} half-hours, {elec['ds'].min():%Y-%m-%d} to {elec['ds'].max():%Y-%m-%d}")
```

```{python}
#| label: elec-overview
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.4), width_ratios=[2, 1])
axes[0].plot(elec["ds"], y_el, color=slate, linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel("GW")
axes[0].set_title("Three and a half months")
week = elec["ds"] >= elec["ds"].iloc[-336]
axes[1].plot(elec.loc[week, "ds"], y_el[week], color=slate, linewidth=1)
axes[1].set_title("The last week")
axes[1].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7, rotation=30)
plt.show()
```

Two seasons visible at once: a **daily** cycle of 48 half-hours and a **weekly** cycle of
$48 \times 7 = 336$. A third, annual, is there too, but four months of data cannot estimate it.

## Why the models so far cannot do this {.smaller}

- **ETS** has one seasonal period, and a seasonal state per position: 336 weekly states to estimate,
  updating one at a time once a week.
- **Seasonal ARIMA** with $m = 336$: a seasonal difference at lag 336 and seasonal terms that multiply
  out to polynomials of degree over a thousand. It fits, slowly, and estimates the weekly pattern from
  a handful of weeks.
- And neither can hold **two** seasonal periods at once.

Two ways out, both built from pieces you already have:

| Approach | Built from | Week |
|---|---|---|
| **MSTL** — decompose into several seasonal components, forecast each simply | STL | 2 |
| **Dynamic harmonic regression** — Fourier terms for each period, ARIMA errors | Fourier terms + dynamic regression | 5, 7 |

## MSTL: STL with several seasons {.smaller}

$$
y_t = T_t + S^{(48)}_t + S^{(336)}_t + R_t
$$

STL applied repeatedly, one seasonal period at a time, from the shortest to the longest.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
mstl = MSTL(season_length=[48, 336]).fit(y=y_el)
components = mstl.model_
components.tail(3)
```

## The components {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: mstl-components
#| fig-align: center
last = slice(len(components) - 3 * 336, None)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(5, 1, figsize=(12, 6.2), sharex=True)
for ax, col, colour in zip(axes, ["data", "trend", "seasonal48", "seasonal336", "remainder"],
                           [slate, blue, turquoise, orange, red_pink]):
    ax.plot(elec["ds"].iloc[last], components[col].iloc[last], color=colour, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_ylabel(col, fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title("MSTL of the last three weeks, GW")
plt.show()
```

The daily shape is the largest component; the weekly one is mostly the weekend dip; the remainder is
what neither season explains — weather, above all.

## MSTL as a forecaster {.smaller}

The forecast is built the way Week 4's decomposition forecast was:

1. each seasonal component is carried forward from its last cycle;
2. the seasonally adjusted series — trend plus remainder — is forecast by a **non-seasonal model**:
   by default `AutoETS(model="ZZN")`;
3. the pieces are added back.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
fc_mstl = MSTL(season_length=[48, 336]).fit(y=y_el[:-336]).predict(h=336, level=[80])
```

It is one line in `statsforecast`, and it is the same idea as Lab 4 — STL plus a simple method for the
level — generalised to more than one season.

## Dynamic harmonic regression {.smaller}

Week 5's Fourier terms, now for **each** seasonal period, and Week 7's ARIMA errors:

$$
y_t = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K_1}\left[\alpha_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k t}{48} + \gamma_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k t}{48}\right]
+ \sum_{k=1}^{K_2}\left[\delta_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi k t}{336} + \lambda_k \cos\tfrac{2\pi k t}{336}\right] + \eta_t
$$

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
t = np.arange(len(y_el) + 336)


def fourier(K, m):
    return np.column_stack([f(2 * np.pi * k * t / m) for k in range(1, K + 1) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)])


X_season = np.column_stack([fourier(10, 48), fourier(5, 336)])     # K = 10 daily, K = 5 weekly
X_weather = np.column_stack([X_season, np.r_[temp, temp[-336:]], np.r_[temp, temp[-336:]] ** 2])
print("regressors:", X_season.shape[1], "seasonal,", X_weather.shape[1] - X_season.shape[1], "for temperature")
```

- The seasons live in the Fourier terms, so the error stays **non-seasonal** and **undifferenced**:
  `AutoARIMA(season_length=1, d=0)`.
- $K$ is chosen, not searched — AICc over-fits long periods (FPP §12.1). Temperature enters as in
  Week 7, ex-post.

## Three weeks ahead, scored {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: elec-scoring
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
H = 336
scale_el = float(np.mean(np.abs(y_el[336:] - y_el[:-336])))
ends = [len(y_el) - k * H for k in (3, 2, 1)]       # three weeks
dhr = partial(AutoARIMA, season_length=1, d=0,
              max_p=3, max_q=3)


def score(forecaster):
    return [float(np.mean(np.abs(y_el[e:e + H] - forecaster(e)))
                  / scale_el) for e in ends]


def mstl_fc(e):
    model = MSTL(season_length=[48, 336]).fit(y=y_el[:e])
    return model.predict(h=H)["mean"]


def dhr_fc(e, X):
    model = dhr().fit(y=y_el[:e], X=X[:e])
    return model.predict(h=H, X=X[e:e + H])["mean"]


elec_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "seasonal naive (week)": score(lambda e: y_el[e - 336:e - 336 + H]),
    "MSTL": score(mstl_fc),
    "harmonic regression": score(lambda e: dhr_fc(e, X_season)),
    "+ temperature": score(lambda e: dhr_fc(e, X_weather)),
}, index=[f"from {elec['ds'].iloc[e]:%m-%d}" for e in ends]).T
elec_scores["mean"] = elec_scores.mean(axis=1)
elec_scores.round(3)
```

## Three weeks ahead, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: elec-forecasts
#| fig-align: center
e = ends[-1]
window = elec["ds"].iloc[e:e + H]
lines = {
    "seasonal naive (week)": (y_el[e - 336:e - 336 + H], red_pink, ":"),
    "MSTL": (mstl_fc(e), turquoise, "-"),
    "+ temperature": (dhr_fc(e, X_weather), orange, "--"),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.2))
ax.plot(elec["ds"].iloc[e - 336:e + H], y_el[e - 336:e + H], color=slate, linewidth=1, label="actual")
for name, (fc, colour, style) in lines.items():
    ax.plot(window, fc, style, color=colour, linewidth=1.4, label=name)
ax.axvline(elec["ds"].iloc[e], color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("GW")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("The last of the three weeks, from its origin")
plt.show()
```

## Complex seasonality: what to take away {.smaller}

- **On average** all three models beat the seasonal naive week, and temperature helps a little. But
  look at the columns: **seasonal naive wins two of the three weeks**. The average is carried by the one
  week where copying last week failed badly. Three windows are close to noise — the honest summary is
  "comparable, with MSTL the cheapest".
- **MSTL** is the first thing to try: one line, seconds to fit, and it reuses decomposition logic you
  know. **Harmonic regression** is the flexible one — any number of seasons, any predictors — but slower,
  and $K$ is a judgement call. (`AutoTBATS`, the third standard option, took 19 minutes on the same
  three weeks and scored worst, 1.98.)
- Neither knows about **holidays**: the week of Christmas, which these three weeks stop just short of,
  breaks every model here. That is a regressor problem, not a seasonality problem.
- Your Track B series are monthly or quarterly: one season. MSTL still applies with one period — and
  is one of the candidates that the next section combines.

# Prophet

## What Prophet is {.smaller}

**Prophet** is an open-source forecasting library released by Facebook (Meta) in 2017 — "forecasting
at scale" (Taylor & Letham, [2017](https://peerj.com/preprints/3190.pdf)).

- **Built for** analysts with domain knowledge but not necessarily time series training, who need many
  forecasts of business series with strong seasonality and several seasons of history.
- **Analyst in the loop:** the model is automatic — robust to missing data, outliers and trend shifts —
  but every component has a handle you can turn by hand: changepoints, capacities, holidays, seasonal
  flexibility.
- It is the most widely installed "advanced" forecasting library. That is a reason to know what it does
  — and to score it before you trust it.

## The model {.smaller}

$$
y(t) = g(t) + s(t) + h(t) + \varepsilon_t
$$

| Term | What it is | You have met it as |
|---|---|---|
| $g(t)$ | a **piecewise** trend with changepoints | Week 5's piecewise linear trend |
| $s(t)$ | **Fourier terms** for each seasonal period | Week 5's Fourier terms |
| $h(t)$ | **holiday** indicators from a calendar | Week 5's dummy variables |
| $\varepsilon_t$ | the error — assumed independent | what Week 7 said not to assume |

::: {.callout-important}
Prophet treats forecasting as **curve fitting**, not as temporal dependence. It does not need regularly
spaced data or interpolated gaps, and it fits fast — but $y_{t-1}$ never enters the forecast of $y_t$.
There is no ARIMA error and no ETS state: short-run dynamics stay in the residuals.
:::

## The classic example: Peyton Manning {.smaller}

Log daily page views of the Wikipedia article on Peyton Manning, 2007–2016 — the example from Prophet's
own documentation.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
peyton = pd.read_csv('../data/peyton_manning.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
print(f"{len(peyton)} days, {peyton['ds'].min():%Y-%m-%d} to {peyton['ds'].max():%Y-%m-%d}")
```

```{python}
#| label: peyton-raw
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax.plot(peyton["ds"], peyton["y"], ".", color=slate, markersize=1.5)
ax.set_ylabel("log views")
ax.set_title("Each NFL season is a peak; each off-season a trough")
plt.show()
```

## Four calls {.smaller}

The interface follows scikit-learn: build, `fit`, extend the dates, `predict`.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
m = Prophet()
m.fit(peyton)
future = m.make_future_dataframe(periods=365)          # one year past the data
forecast = m.predict(future)
forecast[["ds", "yhat", "yhat_lower", "yhat_upper"]].tail(3)
```

## The forecast {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: peyton-forecast
#| fig-align: center
fig = m.plot(forecast, figsize=(12, 4.2))
plt.title("Prophet's default plot: data (dots), forecast (line), 80% interval (band)")
plt.show()
```

## The trend $g(t)$: a line that is allowed to bend {.smaller}

$$
g(t) = \left(k + \mathbf{a}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}\right) t + \left(m + \mathbf{a}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)
$$

- $k$ — the growth rate of the first segment; $m$ — its offset.
- $s_1, \dots, s_S$ — **changepoints**, and $a_j(t) = 1$ once $t \ge s_j$, 0 before.
- $\delta_j$ — the **change in slope** at changepoint $j$. The slope after the last changepoint is
  $k + \sum_j \delta_j$.
- $\gamma_j = -s_j\delta_j$ — not a free parameter: it shifts the offset so the segments **join** at each
  changepoint instead of jumping.

This is Week 5's piecewise trend, $\max(0, t - \tau)$, with many knots instead of one — and with a way
to choose which knots matter.

## Choosing the changepoints {.smaller}

1. **Candidates.** 25 potential changepoints, spread evenly over the first 80% of the history.
2. **A sparse prior.** Each slope change gets a Laplace prior,
   $\delta_j \sim \text{Laplace}(0, \tau)$ — the Bayesian version of a lasso penalty. Most $\delta_j$ end
   up at or near zero; only real changes in slope survive.

```{python}
#| label: peyton-changepoints
#| fig-align: center
fig = m.plot(forecast, figsize=(12, 3.6))
add_changepoints_to_plot(fig.gca(), m, forecast)
plt.title("Red: the changepoints that survived, and the fitted trend")
plt.show()
```

## How flexible should the trend be? {.smaller}

$\tau$ is `changepoint_prior_scale`: large lets the trend bend at every bump, small keeps it nearly
straight.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
flexible = Prophet(changepoint_prior_scale=0.5).fit(peyton)
stiff = Prophet(changepoint_prior_scale=0.001).fit(peyton)
fc_flexible, fc_stiff = flexible.predict(future), stiff.predict(future)
```

```{python}
#| label: peyton-flexibility
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.3))
ax.plot(peyton["ds"], peyton["y"], ".", color="lightgray", markersize=1.5)
ax.plot(fc_flexible["ds"], fc_flexible["trend"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="trend, τ = 0.5")
ax.plot(fc_stiff["ds"], fc_stiff["trend"], color=blue, linewidth=1.8, label="trend, τ = 0.001")
ax.plot(forecast["ds"], forecast["trend"], "--", color=turquoise, linewidth=1.5, label="trend, default τ = 0.05")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

The flexible trend follows the last decline and extrapolates it; the stiff one barely moves. Same data,
very different forecasts a year out — $\tau$ is a forecasting decision, not a fitting detail.

## Forecast uncertainty from the trend {.smaller}

- Past the data there are no changepoints to fit — but the future will have them too.
- Prophet **simulates** them: it estimates how often and how much the slope changed in the past, draws
  future changepoints at that rate and size, and propagates many trend paths.
- The interval is the spread of those paths **plus** the residual noise. So a flexible trend in the
  past gives a wide interval in the future, which is honest: more past changes, less certainty.
- What the interval does **not** include: any autocorrelation of the errors. That is where Prophet's
  intervals are most often too narrow.

## Saturating growth {.smaller}

When growth has a ceiling — a market, a population, a capacity — Prophet can replace the line by a
logistic curve:

$$
g(t) = \frac{C(t)}{1 + \exp\!\left(-\left(k + \mathbf{a}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}\right)\left(t - \left(m + \mathbf{a}(t)^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)\right)\right)}
$$

- $C(t)$ — the **carrying capacity**, which **you supply** as a column `cap` (it may change over time).
- `Prophet(growth="logistic")` — and the same changepoints, now changing the growth rate of the curve.

Like the scaled logit later in this lecture: the bound is an assumption you write down, and the
forecast leans on it.

## The seasonality $s(t)$ {.smaller}

$$
s(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[a_n \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{P}\right) + b_n \sin\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{P}\right)\right]
$$

Exactly Week 5's Fourier terms: $P$ is the period in days, $N$ the number of harmonics. Defaults: yearly
($P = 365.25$, $N = 10$), weekly ($P = 7$, $N = 3$), daily for sub-daily data. Others are added by hand:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
m = Prophet(weekly_seasonality=False)
m.add_seasonality(name="monthly", period=30.5, fourier_order=5)
```

## The components {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: peyton-components
#| fig-align: center
fig = m.plot_components(forecast, figsize=(12, 5.2))
plt.show()
```

Trend, weekly, yearly — each a function you can read: views peak on Mondays after Sunday games, and in
January around the play-offs.

## Holidays and events $h(t)$ {.smaller}

A holiday is a dummy variable — with a **window** of days before and after it, because the effect of
Christmas starts before the 25th. Built-in country calendars, or your own table of events (games,
launches, promotions).

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
with_holidays = Prophet()
with_holidays.add_country_holidays(country_name="US")
with_holidays.fit(peyton)
fc_holidays = with_holidays.predict(future)
print(with_holidays.train_holiday_names.to_list()[:6])
```

For Peyton Manning the effect that matters is the **Super Bowl**, which is not a public holiday. Prophet's
documentation adds playoff and Super Bowl dates as a custom events table — the analyst in the loop.

## Prophet's own cross-validation {.smaller}

Prophet ships a rolling-origin evaluation: `initial` days of training, a new origin every `period`,
`horizon` days ahead — the same idea as Week 3.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
cv_peyton = cross_validation(m, initial="1825 days", period="180 days",
                             horizon="365 days", disable_tqdm=True)
metrics = performance_metrics(cv_peyton, rolling_window=0.1)
metrics[["horizon", "rmse", "mae", "coverage"]].iloc[::60].round(3)
```

`coverage` is the share of actual values inside the 80% interval, by horizon. It sits mostly **below
0.80** — the too-narrow intervals the previous slides predicted for a model without error dynamics.

## Prophet against the models of this course {.smaller}

Two series from this course, scored on the same rolling origins as their earlier comparisons:

```{python}
#| label: cement-helpers
production = pd.read_csv('../data/aus_production.csv',
                         parse_dates=["ds"])
cement = (production.query("ds.dt.year >= 1988")
          [["ds", "Cement"]].dropna()
          .rename(columns={"Cement": "y"})
          .reset_index(drop=True))
y_cem, H_CEM = cement["y"].to_numpy(float), 8
scale_cem = float(np.mean(np.abs(y_cem[4:] - y_cem[:-4])))
cem_ends = [len(y_cem) - H_CEM - 4 * k
            for k in range(5, -1, -1)]          # six origins


def cem_score(fc):
    return np.mean([np.mean(np.abs(y_cem[e:e + H_CEM] - fc(e)))
                    / scale_cem for e in cem_ends])


def prophet_cem(e):
    model = Prophet(weekly_seasonality=False,
                    daily_seasonality=False)
    model.fit(cement.iloc[:e])
    future = cement.iloc[e:e + H_CEM][["ds"]]
    return model.predict(future)["yhat"].to_numpy()


def stats_cem(model):
    return lambda e: model.fit(y=y_cem[:e]).predict(h=H_CEM)["mean"]
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
pd.Series({
    "Prophet": cem_score(prophet_cem),
    "AutoETS": cem_score(stats_cem(AutoETS(season_length=4))),
    "AutoARIMA": cem_score(stats_cem(AutoARIMA(season_length=4))),
    "snaive": cem_score(lambda e: y_cem[e - 4:e][np.arange(H_CEM) % 4]),
}, name="cement, MASE").round(3)
```

## Back to half-hourly electricity {.smaller}

The three weeks from the complex seasonality section, with Prophet added — daily and weekly seasonality
are switched on automatically for sub-daily data:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
elec_df = pd.DataFrame({"ds": elec["ds"], "y": y_el, "temp": temp})


def prophet_elec(e, with_temp):
    model = Prophet(yearly_seasonality=False)
    if with_temp:
        model.add_regressor("temp")
    model.fit(elec_df.iloc[:e])
    window = elec_df.iloc[e:e + H][["ds", "temp"]]
    return model.predict(window)["yhat"].to_numpy()


elec_scores.loc["Prophet"] = score(lambda e: prophet_elec(e, False)) + [np.nan]
elec_scores.loc["Prophet + temperature"] = score(lambda e: prophet_elec(e, True)) + [np.nan]
elec_scores["mean"] = elec_scores.iloc[:, :3].mean(axis=1)
elec_scores.round(3)
```

## What Prophet is, and is not {.smaller}

- **Is:** a convenient regression — piecewise trend, Fourier seasons, holiday windows — with good
  defaults, a readable decomposition, and fast fits. On Peyton Manning, its home ground, it does what it
  was built for.
- **Is not:** a better forecaster by default. On cement it loses to ETS, ARIMA **and** seasonal naive;
  on half-hourly electricity it loses to MSTL and to harmonic regression, and only temperature brings
  it near seasonal naive.
- **Why:** no error dynamics. Everything Weeks 6 and 7 built — using the last few errors — is missing,
  and short horizons are where that costs most.

[Treat Prophet as one more candidate to score on a rolling origin — never as the default.]{.hi}

# Weekly data

## The trouble with $m = 52$ {.smaller}

A year has $365.25 / 7 \approx$ **52.18** weeks. Every method that needs an **integer** seasonal period
is approximately wrong from the start, and drifts by a day and a quarter per year.

- ETS and seasonal ARIMA: $m = 52$ is long, and must be an integer.
- **MSTL with `season_length=52`**: integer too, but the season is estimated by smoothing, not state by
  state.
- **Harmonic regression**: Fourier terms take **any** period, $P = 52.18$ — the one method here for which
  the non-integer year is no problem.

The example: Victoria's electricity demand again, summed to **weekly** totals, 2012–2014.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
weekly = (vic.query("unique_id == 'Demand'").set_index("ds")["y"]
          .resample("W-SUN").sum().iloc[1:-1] / 1e6 / 2)        # full weeks only, TWh
y_wk = weekly.to_numpy(float)
print(f"{len(y_wk)} weeks, {weekly.index.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {weekly.index.max():%Y-%m-%d}")
```

## Weekly electricity: three approaches {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
H_WK = 26                                            # half a year ahead
train_wk, test_wk = y_wk[:-H_WK], y_wk[-H_WK:]
scale_wk = float(np.mean(np.abs(y_wk[52:] - y_wk[:-52])))
t_wk = np.arange(len(y_wk))


def fourier_52(K):
    waves = [f(2 * np.pi * k * t_wk / 52.18)       # P = 52.18
             for k in range(1, K + 1) for f in (np.sin, np.cos)]
    return np.column_stack(waves)


mstl_wk = MSTL(season_length=52).fit(y=train_wk)
weekly_fc = {"seasonal naive (m=52)": train_wk[-52:-52 + H_WK],
             "MSTL (m=52)": mstl_wk.predict(h=H_WK)["mean"]}
for K in (2, 4, 6):
    X = fourier_52(K)
    fit = AutoARIMA(season_length=1).fit(y=train_wk, X=X[:-H_WK])
    weekly_fc[f"harmonic, K={K}"] = fit.predict(h=H_WK, X=X[-H_WK:])["mean"]

pd.Series({k: np.mean(np.abs(test_wk - f)) / scale_wk
           for k, f in weekly_fc.items()}, name="MASE").round(3)
```

## Weekly electricity, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: weekly-elec
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.8))
ax.plot(weekly.index, y_wk, color=slate, linewidth=1, label="weekly demand")
for (name, fc), colour, style in zip([(k, weekly_fc[k]) for k in ("seasonal naive (m=52)", "MSTL (m=52)", "harmonic, K=4")],
                                    [red_pink, turquoise, orange], [":", "-", "--"]):
    ax.plot(weekly.index[-H_WK:], fc, style, color=colour, linewidth=1.8, label=name)
ax.axvline(weekly.index[-H_WK], color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("TWh per week")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

- With **two years** of training data, last year's week is hard to beat: seasonal naive wins. Every
  other method has to estimate the yearly shape from two cycles.
- Harmonic regression comes close with a handful of terms; MSTL, which smooths the season over only two
  cycles, does worst.
- The FPP rule of thumb: **harmonic regression** when the season is stable or you need covariates;
  **STL/MSTL** when the season changes over time and there are enough years to see it change.

# Combining forecasts

## Why combine at all {.smaller}

> "The combination of forecasts often leads to better forecast accuracy" — Bates & Granger (1969),
> confirmed in every large forecasting competition since: M3, M4, M5.

- Different models make **different mistakes**. Averaging cancels part of them.
- Choosing one model on a validation window is itself a **noisy decision** — Week 6 showed a ranking
  that flipped between windows.
- The simplest combination is the best-documented: **the plain average**. Estimated weights rarely beat
  it, because estimating weights is another noisy decision.

$$
\hat y^{\,\text{comb}}_{T+h} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k} \hat y^{(j)}_{T+h}
$$

## Three series, five forecasts {.smaller}

The monthly employment series from the ARIMA lectures — none of them in the Track B pool — scored on
five years of rolling origins:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
employment = pd.read_csv('../data/us_employment.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
models = [AutoETS(season_length=12, alias="ETS"),
          AutoARIMA(season_length=12, alias="ARIMA"),
          AutoTheta(season_length=12, alias="Theta"),
          SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, alias="snaive")]
tables = {}
for name, start in [("Leisure and Hospitality", 2001),
                    ("Retail Trade", 1990), ("Construction", 1990)]:
    df = (employment.query("unique_id == @name and ds.dt.year >= @start")
          .reset_index(drop=True))
    cv = StatsForecast(models=models, freq="MS").cross_validation(
        df=df, h=12, n_windows=5, step_size=12)
    cv["ETS+ARIMA"] = (cv["ETS"] + cv["ARIMA"]) / 2
    cv["ETS+ARIMA+Theta"] = (cv["ETS"] + cv["ARIMA"] + cv["Theta"]) / 3
    tables[name.split()[0]] = scored(cv, df, 12)["MASE"]
pd.DataFrame(tables)
```

## Rarely the best, never the worst {.smaller}

- On all three series **ARIMA alone is best**, and both combinations land **between** the models they
  average.
- That is not a failure of combining. If you *knew* ARIMA would win, you would use it. The question is
  what happens when you do not know — which is every time you forecast something new.
- A combination's forecast error is never larger than the larger error of its parts. Selection can be.

[One series cannot answer "select or combine". You need many — and you have 140.]{.hi}

## Select or combine: 140 series {.smaller}

On every issued Track B series: either **select** between `AutoETS` and `AutoARIMA` on three windows of
the served history (the Lab 5 and Lab 6 way), or **average** them. Both scored on the hidden horizon
against each series' benchmark.

| Strategy | Beats the benchmark | Median skill | Mean skill | Worst skill |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `AutoETS` alone | 100% | 0.835 | 0.840 | 0.999 |
| `AutoARIMA` alone | 100% | 0.809 | 0.816 | 0.999 |
| select the better on validation | 100% | 0.815 | 0.826 | 0.995 |
| **average ETS and ARIMA** | 100% | **0.805** | **0.793** | **0.933** |

## Select or combine: what the table says {.smaller}

- Selection picks the model that turns out better on the hidden horizon on **54%** of series — barely
  better than a coin. Three validation windows do not say much about the next one.
- The average beats selection on **65%** of series, has the better mean, and a much better **worst
  case**: 0.93 against 0.995, where selection came within half a percent of losing a point.
- If you could always pick the better model, the median would be 0.787. Nobody can; the average gets
  most of the way there without trying.

## Combining other models {.smaller}

The same pool, more members:

| Forecast | Beats the benchmark | Median skill |
|---|---:|---:|
| `AutoETS` | 100% | 0.835 |
| `AutoARIMA` | 100% | 0.809 |
| **ETS + ARIMA** | **100%** | **0.805** |
| ETS + ARIMA + Theta | 92% | 0.796 |
| `MSTL` alone | 80% | 0.812 |
| `AutoCES` alone | 79% | 0.840 |
| `AutoTheta` alone | 67% | 0.855 |

- Adding Theta lowers the median a little and **raises the risk**: it is the weakest member, and it
  drags the bad cases down with it.
- A combination is as good as the worst member it cannot outvote. Combine models that are each
  defensible on their own.

## A combination, built step by step {.smaller}

US leisure employment once more, with a fixed three-way split: **train** to September 2014, a
**validation** window from October 2014 to September 2016, and a **test** window of the last 36 months.
Three different model families:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
leisure = (employment.query("unique_id == 'Leisure and Hospitality' and ds.dt.year >= 2001")
           .reset_index(drop=True))
y_lei = leisure["y"].to_numpy(float) / 1000                       # millions of people
N_TEST, N_VAL = 36, 24
train_lei, valid_lei, test_lei = y_lei[:-(N_TEST + N_VAL)], y_lei[-(N_TEST + N_VAL):-N_TEST], y_lei[-N_TEST:]
members = {"ETS": lambda: AutoETS(season_length=12),
           "ARIMA": lambda: AutoARIMA(season_length=12),
           "MSTL": lambda: MSTL(season_length=12)}

# the members, refitted on train + validation, forecasting the test window
test_fc = {name: make().fit(y=np.r_[train_lei, valid_lei]).predict(h=N_TEST, level=[80])
           for name, make in members.items()}
combination = np.mean([fc["mean"] for fc in test_fc.values()], axis=0)
print({name: round(float(np.mean(np.abs(test_lei - fc["mean"]))), 3) for name, fc in test_fc.items()},
      "| combination:", round(float(np.mean(np.abs(test_lei - combination))), 3), "(MAE, millions)")
```

## Two ways to an interval {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# 1. Average the members' own 80% bounds.
avg_lo = np.mean([fc["lo-80"] for fc in test_fc.values()], axis=0)
avg_hi = np.mean([fc["hi-80"] for fc in test_fc.values()], axis=0)

# 2. Conformal: errors of the combination on the validation window, added to the new forecast.
valid_fc = np.mean([make().fit(y=train_lei).predict(h=N_VAL)["mean"] for make in members.values()], axis=0)
valid_errors = valid_lei - valid_fc
conf_lo = combination + np.quantile(valid_errors, 0.10)
conf_hi = combination + np.quantile(valid_errors, 0.90)
print(f"validation errors of the combination: mean {valid_errors.mean():+.3f}, "
      f"10% quantile {np.quantile(valid_errors, 0.1):+.3f}, 90% quantile {np.quantile(valid_errors, 0.9):+.3f}")
```

The conformal recipe needs no model: whatever the combination's errors were on held-out data, assume the
next ones look the same. That assumption is the whole method — and the next slide tests it.

## Scoring intervals: the Winkler score {.smaller}

An interval can fail two ways: too wide to be useful, or too narrow to contain the truth. The **Winkler
score** charges for both — the width, plus a penalty for every miss. Lower is better.

$$
W_\alpha(\ell_t, u_t, y_t) =
\begin{cases}
(u_t - \ell_t) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(\ell_t - y_t) & y_t < \ell_t \\
(u_t - \ell_t) & \ell_t \le y_t \le u_t \\
(u_t - \ell_t) + \frac{2}{\alpha}(y_t - u_t) & y_t > u_t
\end{cases}
$$

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
def winkler(y, lo, hi, alpha=0.2):
    below, above = np.maximum(lo - y, 0), np.maximum(y - hi, 0)
    return float(np.mean((hi - lo) + 2 / alpha * (below + above)))


def coverage(y, lo, hi):
    return float(np.mean((y >= lo) & (y <= hi)))
```

## The five intervals, scored {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
intervals = {f"{name}'s own": (fc["lo-80"], fc["hi-80"])
             for name, fc in test_fc.items()}
intervals["combination, averaged bounds"] = (avg_lo, avg_hi)
intervals["combination, conformal"] = (conf_lo, conf_hi)

pd.DataFrame({
    name: {"coverage": coverage(test_lei, lo, hi),
           "Winkler": winkler(test_lei, lo, hi)}
    for name, (lo, hi) in intervals.items()
}).T.round(3)
```

## What the intervals did {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: combination-intervals
#| fig-align: center
test_dates = leisure["ds"].iloc[-N_TEST:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.6))
ax.plot(leisure["ds"].iloc[-(N_TEST + 48):], y_lei[-(N_TEST + 48):], color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="actual")
ax.plot(test_dates, combination, color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="combination")
ax.fill_between(test_dates, avg_lo, avg_hi, color=turquoise, alpha=0.25, label="averaged 80% bounds")
ax.fill_between(test_dates, conf_lo, conf_hi, color=orange, alpha=0.35, label="conformal 80%, one validation window")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_ylabel("millions")
plt.show()
```

- The combination's **point forecast** is as accurate as the best member, without knowing in advance which member that would be.
- The **conformal** interval sits **above** the forecast — it does not even contain it. The validation
  window was one where the members under-forecast, and the method copied that bias into the future.
- The averaged bounds cover every month and have the **best Winkler score** of all five. Neither recipe
  is right in general: a conformal interval needs errors from **many** windows, not one.

# Forecasts within limits

## Egg prices, thirty years ahead {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
eggs = pd.read_csv('../data/egg_prices.csv', parse_dates=["ds"])
y_egg = eggs["y"].to_numpy(float)
h_egg = 30
raw = RandomWalkWithDrift().fit(y=y_egg).predict(h=h_egg, level=[95])
logged = {k: np.exp(v) for k, v in RandomWalkWithDrift().fit(y=np.log(y_egg)).predict(h=h_egg, level=[95]).items()}
print(f"raw drift:  forecast in 30 years {raw['mean'][-1]:6.1f}   lower 95% bound {raw['lo-95'][-1]:7.1f}")
print(f"log drift:  forecast in 30 years {logged['mean'][-1]:6.1f}   lower 95% bound {logged['lo-95'][-1]:7.1f}")
print(f"raw drift's lower bound is negative from step {int(np.argmax(raw['lo-95'] < 0)) + 1}")
```

```{python}
#| label: eggs
#| fig-align: center
future = pd.date_range(eggs["ds"].iloc[-1], periods=h_egg + 1, freq="YS")[1:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.4))
ax.plot(eggs["ds"], y_egg, color=slate, label="egg price, constant dollars")
for fc, colour, name in [(raw, red_pink, "drift on the price"), (logged, turquoise, "drift on log, back-transformed")]:
    ax.plot(future, fc["mean"], color=colour, linewidth=1.8, label=name)
    ax.fill_between(future, fc["lo-95"], fc["hi-95"], color=colour, alpha=0.15)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()
```

## Logs keep forecasts positive {.smaller}

- A drift on the **price** extrapolates a straight line down, and it crosses zero. A drift on the **log**
  extrapolates a constant *rate* of decline, which never reaches zero — and its interval is
  asymmetric, as a price's should be.
- **Back-transforming gives the median, not the mean.** $\exp(\widehat{\log y})$ is the middle of the
  forecast distribution; the mean is higher. For a forecast scored on squared error, that matters —
  FPP §5.6 gives the bias adjustment.
- The same trick works for ETS and ARIMA: fit on $\log y$, exponentiate the forecast and the bounds.
  Lab 6's template did exactly that.

## Between two limits: the scaled logit {.smaller}

When a quantity is bounded on **both** sides — a share in $[0, 1]$, a price that has a floor and a
ceiling — transform with

$$
z = \log\frac{y - a}{b - y}, \qquad y = \frac{(b - a)\,e^{z}}{1 + e^{z}} + a
$$

Forecast $z$ with any model, back-transform, and every point of the forecast and its interval lies in
$(a, b)$.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
a, b = 50, 400
z = np.log((y_egg - a) / (b - y_egg))
fz = RandomWalkWithDrift().fit(y=z).predict(h=h_egg, level=[95])
back = lambda q: (b - a) * np.exp(q) / (1 + np.exp(q)) + a
print(f"in 30 years: {back(fz['mean'])[-1]:.1f}, 95% interval [{back(fz['lo-95'])[-1]:.1f}, {back(fz['hi-95'])[-1]:.1f}]")
```

The bounds are an **assumption you write down**, not something the data tell you — and the forecast
leans on them: here the lower bound of 50 is what stops the decline.

# Mostly zeros

## Time series of counts {.smaller}

Every model so far treats $y$ as **continuous**. Much real data is **counts**: customers, items sold,
scripts dispensed.

- **Large counts** — hundreds and up — are fine: the difference between 100 and 100.4 does not matter.
- **Small counts** — 0, 1, 2, 3 — matter: a forecast of 0.4 items is not a quantity anyone can stock,
  and a symmetric normal interval spills below zero.
- **Intermittent demand** — mostly zeros — is the extreme case, and the one with dedicated methods.

## Intermittent demand {.smaller}

Spare parts, slow-moving stock, rare events: most periods are **zero**, and when demand arrives, it
varies. A simulated example — three years of weekly demand for one part:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n, H_int = 156, 13
occurs = rng.random(n + H_int) < 0.25                  # demand in about one week in four
demand = np.where(occurs, rng.poisson(4, n + H_int) + 1, 0).astype(float)
history, future_demand = demand[:n], demand[n:]
print(f"zero weeks: {np.mean(history == 0):.0%}   mean weekly demand: {history.mean():.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: intermittent
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.6))
ax.bar(np.arange(n), history, color=slate, width=0.8)
ax.bar(np.arange(n, n + H_int), future_demand, color=red_pink, width=0.8, label="the 13 weeks we forecast")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_xlabel("week")
plt.show()
```

## Croston's method {.smaller}

Split the series into two, and smooth each with SES:

- $q$ — the **size** of demand when it occurs;
- $a$ — the **interval** between occurrences.

$$
\hat y_{T+h|T} = \frac{\hat q_T}{\hat a_T} \qquad \text{— a demand rate per period, flat over the horizon}
$$

- The forecast is never zero, and never a spike: it is the **average rate**, which is what a stock
  decision needs.
- **SBA** corrects Croston's known upward bias; **TSB** smooths the *probability* of demand instead of
  the interval, so the rate can decay when a part stops selling.

## How to score it {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| output-location: column
candidates = {"zero": ZeroModel(), "naive": Naive(), "mean": HistoricAverage(),
              "Croston": CrostonClassic(), "SBA": CrostonSBA(),
              "TSB": TSB(alpha_d=0.2, alpha_p=0.2)}
rows = []
for name, model in candidates.items():
    fc = np.asarray(model.fit(y=history).predict(h=H_int)["mean"], float)
    rows.append({"forecast": name, "weekly rate": fc[0],
                 "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(future_demand - fc)),
                 "RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((future_demand - fc) ** 2)),
                 "13-week total error": abs(fc.sum() - future_demand.sum())})
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2)
```

- **MAE is won by "zero".** The median of a mostly-zero series is zero, and MAE rewards the median —
  so the metric recommends stocking nothing.
- RMSE and the **total over the horizon** reward the rate, which is what the warehouse orders.
- MASE inherits the problem from MAE. For intermittent series: RMSE, or a total-demand error.

# Backcasting

## Forecasting the past {.smaller}

Sometimes the gap is at the **start**: a series begins in 2001, and you need 1999 and 2000 — to
splice two sources, or to fill a history before a model can use it.

**Backcasting** = reverse the series, forecast it forward, reverse the forecast. Every model in this
course works unchanged, because time series models do not know which way time runs.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
reversed_fit = AutoETS(season_length=12).fit(y=y_lei[::-1])
back = {k: v[::-1] for k, v in reversed_fit.predict(h=24, level=[80]).items()}
back_dates = pd.date_range(end=leisure["ds"].iloc[0] - pd.DateOffset(months=1), periods=24, freq="MS")
```

Here the past exists — the series goes back to 1939 — so the backcast can be **checked**:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
actual_past = (employment.query("unique_id == 'Leisure and Hospitality'")
               .set_index("ds").loc[back_dates, "y"].to_numpy(float) / 1000)
print(f"MAE {np.mean(np.abs(actual_past - back['mean'])):.3f} million   "
      f"80% interval covered {coverage(actual_past, back['lo-80'], back['hi-80']):.0%} of the 24 months")
```

## The backcast, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: backcast
#| fig-align: center
context = employment.query("unique_id == 'Leisure and Hospitality' and ds.dt.year >= 1997 and ds.dt.year <= 2004")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.8))
ax.plot(context["ds"], context["y"] / 1000, color="lightgray", linewidth=1.5, label="what actually happened")
ax.plot(leisure["ds"].iloc[:48], y_lei[:48], color=slate, linewidth=1.2, label="the data the model saw")
ax.plot(back_dates, back["mean"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="backcast")
ax.fill_between(back_dates, back["lo-80"], back["hi-80"], color=red_pink, alpha=0.2, label="80% interval")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
ax.set_ylabel("millions")
plt.show()
```

The backcast reproduces the seasonal shape and the level; the trend it runs backwards is the post-2001
one. Backcasts deserve the same suspicion as forecasts — the further back, the wider the interval
should be, and the more the past may have been a different regime.

# In practice

## Seven ways to get this wrong {.tiny}

| Trap | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| A long seasonal period forced into ETS or SARIMA | Slow fits, a season estimated from a few cycles | MSTL, or harmonic regression |
| $K$ chosen by AICc for $m = 336$ | Dozens of harmonics, a noisy seasonal shape | Choose $K$; check it on a holdout |
| Selecting one model on one window | A ranking that flips the next window | Combine, or select on several windows |
| A transformed forecast reported as a mean | A forecast biased low on squared error | Say "median", or bias-adjust |
| MAE on intermittent demand | "Zero" wins | RMSE, or the total over the horizon |
| Prophet's defaults trusted as a forecast | Smooth fit, losing to seasonal naive on the holdout | Score it on a rolling origin like any candidate |
| A conformal interval from one validation window | An interval that misses the forecast itself | Errors from many windows |

## What this lecture is, in one slide {.smaller}

- **Complex seasonality** is decomposition or regression with more than one season: MSTL and harmonic
  regression, built from Weeks 2, 5 and 7.
- **Combining** is the cheapest robust improvement in forecasting: rarely the best on one series,
  hardly ever bad across many.
- **Limits** are handled by transforming, forecasting, and transforming back — logs for positivity, the
  scaled logit for two bounds.
- **Intermittent demand** needs a rate, not a path — and a metric that does not reward forecasting
  nothing.
- **Prophet** is Week 5's regression with good defaults and no error model: convenient, readable, and
  on this lecture's series beaten by the models you already have.
- **Weekly data** want Fourier terms, because a year is 52.18 weeks; **backcasting** is forecasting with
  the series reversed.

## In the practice session {.smaller}

**Tomorrow's practice** is the worked example for **Lab 7: seasonal ARIMA**, from the *ARIMA Models,
Part 2* lecture, on your own series. Accuracy is marked again.

**Next week, Lab 8** is today's material on the same series. Your series has one season and no zeros,
so the tool that applies is **combining** — the models you have built over Labs 5–7, with MSTL as a
further candidate — chosen and checked on a rolling origin.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Before Week 9

Read [FPP3 §13.4](https://otexts.com/fpp3/combinations.html). Then take your Lab 5 ETS and your Lab 7
ARIMA, average their forecasts on your validation window, and look where the average lands.
:::
